Green Spain

9 guides
Bizkaiko TxakolinaDO · 3-minute readBizkaia has a humid Atlantic climate with cool summers and little sun. Its wines are lower in alcohol and higher in acidity than those of nearby zones. CangasVino de Calidad · 2-minute readVines grow on steep slate slopes in the southwest of Asturias, with cold winters and very hot summers. Albarín Blanco is the preferred white grape. Getariako TxakolinaDO · 3-minute read95% of the vineyards are less than 1 km from the sea. The wine is a fresh, light Txakoli, characteristic of this zone. Arabako TxakolinaDO · 2-minute readA valley in northern Álava with an Atlantic climate. Its txakoli has a characteristic acidity, with light bitter tones in the aftertaste. Rías BaixasDO · 3-minute readMild, wet Atlantic weather meets poor granite soils, and more than 96% of the grapes harvested are Albariño. It makes a lot of sugar and keeps an acidity that very few grapes in the world reach. Ribeira SacraDO · 3-minute readVines grow on terraced canyon walls above the Miño and the Sil, on soils from granite to slate. The climate is more continental than Atlantic.

Castilla y León

16 guides
BierzoDO · 4-minute readBierzo sits in a basin ringed by mountains, with a climate that mixes the oceanic and the continental. It gets more rain than the so-called dry Spain, and more than 300 hours of sun on average in July and August. LeónDO · 4-minute readOn a summer day in León the days can be very hot, and the night is much colder. That swing builds the natural acidity behind the fresh rosés of Prieto Picudo. ArlanzaDO · 4-minute readArlanza's vineyards sit between 750 and 1,200 m, where day and night temperatures differ sharply. The grapes ripen slowly for almost 60 days, and their skins thicken and load up with polyphenols and aroma. Valles de BenaventeVino de Calidad · 2-minute readPrieto Picudo grows here in an arid climate with very cold winters, on poor soil that drains well. Its wines show red fruit and a touch of aguja, a slight spritz. CigalesDO · 3-minute readThe vines sit halfway down the Pisuerga, between the intense cold of its source and the mildness of its mouth. There soil and climate work together to give grapes with balanced acidity and sugar. Ribera del DueroDO · 3-minute readRibera del Duero sits high, with dry summers and cold nights. While the grapes ripen, day and night are often 15 to 20°C apart. That long, slow ripening builds the compounds that matter by day and sweetens the tannin naturally.

Rioja

4 guides
RiojaDOCa · 4-minute readTwo climates that rarely meet share one sheltered valley. That is where Rioja's wines get their body, their colour and their acidity. Rioja AltaZone of Rioja · 1-minute readThe Atlantic sets the tone here. More rain and fewer hours of sun than further south keep the wines' acidity high. Rioja AlavesaZone of Rioja · 1-minute readHere the Atlantic and the Mediterranean meet, and the shelter of the Sierra de Cantabria counts even more than in Rioja Alta. Rioja OrientalZone of Rioja · 1-minute readThe Mediterranean end of Rioja: drier and warmer, with the most sun.

Navarra and Aragón

11 guides
Pago de OtazuVino de Pago · 1-minute readPago de Otazu lies on a valley floor under strong Atlantic influence. That Atlantic touch and the valley-floor site give the vines a long growing cycle, which brings acidity, colour and balance to the wines. Prado de IrachePrado de IracheVino de Pago · 2-minute readPrado de Irache lies in a Mediterranean climate, yet the Atlantic reaches it strongly enough to set its wine apart from its neighbours. That cooler, damper weather, together with loose ground, explains the acidity that marks its red. Pago de ArínzanoVino de Pago · 2-minute readArínzano's stony soils, low in clay, help give its wines high colour intensity and notable acidity. Mineral notes stand out in them. NavarraDO · 4-minute readNavarra sits far to the north within the Iberian Peninsula, and the climate that comes with that position gives its wines a higher acidity than other traditional regions, even with the same grapes. That acidity shows up as a marked freshness and a great sense of balance. SomontanoDO · 4-minute readSomontano's commonest soils, calcisols and gipsisols, ensure wines with alcohol, fruit and high acidity. Together with a strong swing between day and night temperatures in August and September, they favour the intense aroma of the wines. Campo de BorjaDO · 4-minute readIn Campo de Borja the cierzo, a cold and dry wind, pulls so much moisture from the soil that the vines live under permanent water stress. With little water and a harsh climate, phenolic ripening (the ripening of skins and seeds) is very slow, and that boosts aroma and deep colour in the wines.

Cataluña

12 guides
EmpordàDO · 8-minute readA cold, dry wind from the north often gusts at over 120 km/h across Empordà's vineyards. It keeps the grapes healthy until harvest, and it shaped which varieties grow here. Costers del SegreDO · 4-minute readTemperatures here can swing by up to 25 °C, especially while the grapes ripen. Cold nights in that season give wines of high acidity and intense flavour. Pla de BagesDO · 6-minute readPla de Bages has a climate halfway between Mediterranean and inland continental, and forest and aromatic herbs surround most of its vines. The climate allows light wines with a good acid core, and the smell of those herbs gets into their primary aromas. AlellaDO · 4-minute readAlella's vines grow on sauló, the small grains that granite breaks into at the surface, and it drains so well that the vine has to root deep for water. The white wines show fruit and fresh mineral notes, and they end on a bitter, citrus finish. Conca de BarberàDO · 3-minute readConca de Barberà has a Mediterranean climate in transition between the mild coast and the continental inland, with a marked difference in temperature between day and night. Its native grape, Trepat, is grown almost only here and gives rosados, reds and pink sparkling and needle wines a character all their own. CavaDO · 3-minute readCava is named after the underground caves where the bottles rested, at about 13 to 15 °C all year. Such cellars let the second fermentation run slowly, and as the wine ages, its yeast breaks down and adds delicate aromas.

Valencia and Murcia

11 guides
El TerrerazoEl TerrerazoVino de Pago · 1-minute readThe temperature swing in this vineyard gives the wine its typical colour. It also sets how well its acidity is balanced. ValenciaDO · 4-minute readValencia's wines have high aromatic intensity because the vines suffer water stress in spring and summer, when temperatures are high and evapotranspiration is most marked. Their marked depth of colour comes from the considerable swing in temperature. Utiel-RequenaDO · 4-minute readUtiel-Requena makes its rosados by tipping a new load of crushed, undrained grapes onto the solids left after the first must runs off. The result is a rosado of a colour intensity not reached in other regions, and a high total acidity that gives it freshness and protects it in storage. Los BalaguesesLos BalaguesesVino de Pago · 3-minute readThe vineyard sits on a slope that drains water and makes the most of the vines' exposure to the sun. That favours ripening and a high output of polyphenols, which then go into the colour and body of the wines. YeclaDO · 3-minute readYecla's link to its wine comes mainly from a very dry climate, very arid soils and the mountains that cut it off from the coast and the north. Add strong sunshine and Monastrell gives wines of good colour and plenty of alcohol. JumillaDO · 4-minute readUnder Jumilla's hard conditions, Monastrell gives a robust red wine with deep colour. Its Monastrell liqueur wines are high in tannin, with colour from medium to very high, close to opaque, a result of the area's high temperatures.

Meseta

25 guides
MondéjarDO · 2-minute readDeep red soil, rich in potassium, under temperatures that swing widely through the year. Whites from Malvar and Torrontés stand out. Vinos de MadridDO · 2-minute readYields here are normally low, about 3,000 kg per hectare on average against 8,000 kg allowed. The same land gives deep colour in the reds and aromas of ripe or very ripe fruit. CalzadillaCalzadillaVino de Pago · 2-minute readA cool vineyard on very limy, strongly alkaline ground ripens its grapes slowly and evenly. The wines are red only, deep in colour and rich in polyphenols. MéntridaDO · 2-minute readAn extreme continental climate meets sandy, acidic soil with very little lime. Together they give warm wines, high in alcohol. UclésDO · 2-minute readUclés vineyards climb to 1,200 m, on soil rich in potassium. Both help give very balanced wines suited to a longer life in bottle. Dominio de ValdepusaDominio de ValdepusaVino de Pago · 2-minute readClay on top and pure limestone underneath: the two layers of one estate's soil each leave their mark on the glass.

Andalucía

8 guides
Montilla-MorilesDO · 4-minute readThe vineyards lie in the part of central Andalucía that records the highest July and August temperatures in the Iberian Peninsula, with historic highs above 46 °C. That climate shapes the style of the wines, from the generosos, wines of high natural alcohol, to sweet wines made from grapes dried in the sun. GranadaDO · 4-minute readVines in Granada bud late and ripen slowly between late August and early October. The gap between the day's highs and lows helps the skins and seeds ripen, and polyphenols, the molecules behind a wine's colour and structure, build up in both. Condado de HuelvaDO · 4-minute readThe wine is made and aged on flat or gently rolling land beside Doñana National Park, in a Mediterranean climate with oceanic touches, which show in the wines. The cellars are built to hold 15 to 22 °C all year while the wine ages. MálagaDO · 6-minute readMálaga lies at the southernmost point of Europe's Mediterranean shore, and its many hours of sun give a high potential for ripening and overripening grapes. Mountains and the sea buffer the temperatures, which gives finesse and keeps the varietal aromas. Sierras de MálagaDO · 3-minute readEurope's most southerly mountains rise in this zone, and their spurs run south to the Mediterranean. Ripening temperatures stay moderate, with a drop at night, because the heat of the latitude is held in check. LebrijaVino de Calidad · 4-minute readLebrija's vines grow on flat farmland right beside the Guadalquivir marshes. The wines carry a subtle note that is sometimes described as salty.

Balearic Islands

2 guides
BinissalemDO · 2-minute readOn Mallorca, climate and ground help the local grapes ripen fully. Binissalem makes still and sparkling wine from that fruit. Pla i LlevantDO · 2-minute readSun and a salty sea wind shape these island wines. They give concentrated aromas, high alcohol and an integrated acidity that brings structure and vigour.

Canary Islands

11 guides
LanzaroteDO · 4-minute readLanzarote's vines grow in a near-desert, under a layer of volcanic ash that holds the moisture in the air. Their wines have a marked volcanic-mineral taste, balanced by relatively high acidity. La PalmaDO · 4-minute readIn Hoyo de Mazo and Fuencaliente, vines creep over volcanic stones and picón, the local volcanic ash, and one plant can reach 36 metres long. The soil gives these wines a salty taste in the mouth. Tacoronte-AcentejoDO · 3-minute readOn Tenerife's north side the vines have a long growing season and ripen slowly, because the temperature barely changes and there is no risk of frost. That slow ripening gives the wines good aromatic intensity and a wide range of colours. Valle de GüímarDO · 4-minute readThe notes of tropical fruit in these wines come from the valley's climate and its high level of sunshine. Izaña, up in its high mountains, records more hours of sun a year than anywhere else in Spain. Valle de la OrotavaDO · 4-minute readMild, humid air bathes this valley all year. That gentle weather, with volcanic soil and long braided vines, is why its wines are fresh and persistent, with low acidity. Ycoden-Daute-IsoraDO · 4-minute readBelow Teide, deep soils full of sand hold very little water and warm up sooner than finer soils. So the grapes start ripening earlier and ripen more slowly, and that long, steady ripening gives the wine a perfect balance.
